from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Coordinates are relative to an observer.",
            "A robot finds a box's location.",
            "Changing the grid alters the description.",
            "Physical location remains constant.",
            "Language changes, reality stays the same."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Intuitive Hook: The Observer's Perspective", lecture_lines)
        
        # Setup visual elements
        axes = Axes(x_range=[-2, 5], y_range=[-2, 5], axis_config={"include_tip": True}).scale(0.5)
        self.place_in_area(axes, 'A1', 'F6', scale_factor=0.6)
        
        v = Vector([2, 3], color=BLUE)
        self.place_at_grid(v, 'C3')
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        self.play(Create(axes), GrowArrow(v))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        robot = Dot(color=RED).next_to(v.get_end(), UP, buff=0.1)
        self.add(robot)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(GREEN))
        rotated_axes = axes.copy().rotate(PI/6, about_point=axes.c2p(0, 0))
        self.play(ReplacementTransform(axes.copy(), rotated_axes))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(ORANGE))
        self.play(Indicate(v, color=WHITE))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(PURPLE))
        self.wait(1)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite Review: Basis as Building Blocks", 
                          ["A basis is our building block.", 
                           "Vectors must be linearly independent.", 
                           "Standard basis uses cardinal directions."])
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Display the standard basis vectors i, j (color #FFFFFF)
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFFFF")
        
        origin = self.grid["D4"]
        i_vec = Arrow(origin, origin + RIGHT * 1.5, color=WHITE, buff=0)
        j_vec = Arrow(origin, origin + UP * 1.5, color=WHITE, buff=0)
        
        i_label = MathTex(r"\mathbf{i}", color=WHITE).next_to(i_vec.get_end(), RIGHT, buff=0.1)
        j_label = MathTex(r"\mathbf{j}", color=WHITE).next_to(j_vec.get_end(), UP, buff=0.1)
        
        self.play(Create(i_vec), Create(j_vec), Write(i_label), Write(j_label))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Form a grid using i, j as the basis
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFFFFF")
        
        grid = NumberPlane(
            x_range=(-2, 2, 1), y_range=(-2, 2, 1),
            x_length=3, y_length=3,
            background_line_style={"stroke_color": GREY, "stroke_width": 1}
        ).move_to(origin)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(grid), run_time=1.5)
        self.bring_to_front(i_vec, j_vec, i_label, j_label)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Introduce a new basis {b1, b2} (color #00FF00) as vectors
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00FF00")
        
        b1 = Arrow(origin, origin + (RIGHT + 0.5 * UP) * 1.5, color=GREEN, buff=0)
        b2 = Arrow(origin, origin + (-0.5 * RIGHT + UP) * 1.5, color=GREEN, buff=0)
        
        b1_label = MathTex(r"\mathbf{b}_1", color=GREEN).next_to(b1.get_end(), RIGHT, buff=0.1)
        b2_label = MathTex(r"\mathbf{b}_2", color=GREEN).next_to(b2.get_end(), UP, buff=0.1)
        
        self.play(Create(b1), Create(b2), Write(b1_label), Write(b2_label))
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("The Change of Basis Matrix (The 'Translator')", [
            "Need a translator between bases.",
            "Columns are the new basis vectors.",
            "Matrix P connects different grid overlays.",
            "Convert [v]_B to [v]_A.",
            "Compute [v]_A equals P times [v]_B."
        ])
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Need a translator between bases.
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#00FFFF")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Columns are the new basis vectors.
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#00FFFF")
        # Creating P matrix: [[1, 0], [1, 1]]
        p_matrix = Matrix([[1, 0], [1, 1]]).set_color("#00FFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(p_matrix, 'B2', scale_factor=0.6)
        self.play(Create(p_matrix))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Matrix P connects different grid overlays.
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00FFFF")
        label = Text("P", font_size=24, color="#00FFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(label, 'B1')
        self.play(Write(label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # Convert [v]_B to [v]_A.
        self.lecture[3].set_color("#00FFFF")
        v_b = MathTex(r"[v]_B").set_color("#FF00FF")
        self.place_at_grid(v_b, 'D2', scale_factor=0.8)
        self.play(FadeIn(v_b))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # Compute [v]_A equals P times [v]_B.
        self.lecture[4].set_color("#00FFFF")
        equation = MathTex(r"[v]_A = P \cdot [v]_B").set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.place_in_area(equation, 'D3', 'F5', scale_factor=0.8)
        self.play(Write(equation))
        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["How do we reverse the translation?", "P-inverse takes us back to A.", "Grid stretches and shears together."]
        self.setup_layout("Visualizing the Inverse", lecture_lines)
        
        # Define base matrix visualization elements
        matrix_p = MathTex(r"P = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}", color="#00FFFF")
        matrix_inv = MathTex(r"P^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & -0.5 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}", color="#FF00FF")
        
        # Grid representation (using lines)
        grid_lines = VGroup()
        for i in range(-2, 3):
            line_h = Line(start=np.array([-1, 0, 0]), end=np.array([1, 0, 0]), color=GRAY)
            line_v = Line(start=np.array([0, -1, 0]), end=np.array([0, 1, 0]), color=GRAY)
            grid_lines.add(line_h.shift(i * 0.4 * UP), line_v.shift(i * 0.4 * RIGHT))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#00FFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(matrix_p, "B4")
        self.play(Write(matrix_p))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FF00FF")
        self.place_at_grid(matrix_inv, "D4")
        self.play(FadeIn(matrix_inv))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)
        self.place_in_area(grid_lines, "B5", "E6", scale_factor=0.8)
        self.play(Create(grid_lines))
        
        # Animate "stretch and shear"
        self.play(
            grid_lines.animate.apply_matrix([[0.5, -0.5], [0, 1]]),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: Mastering the Change of Basis in Linear Algebra

sections.title: Intuitive Hook: The Observer's Perspective
sections.content: Introduce the concept that coordinates are relative to an observer (the basis). Use a 'Robot Delivery' analogy: The robot needs to find a box. If we change the 'grid' the robot uses to see the world, the coordinate numbers change, but the physical location remains identical.
sections.example: A robot at coordinate (2, 3) in Basis A. If we rotate the grid to Basis B, the robot is still at the same spot, but now reads as (1, 4). The 'where' is constant; the 'description' changes.

sections.title: Prerequisite Review: Basis as Building Blocks
sections.content: Briefly define a basis as a set of linearly independent vectors that span the space. Use a visual representation of the Standard Basis (i, j) vs. a Non-Standard Basis (u, v) represented by vectors pointing in different directions.
sections.example: Standard Basis vectors are like the cardinal directions (North, East). A new basis is like using (Northeast, Northwest) to describe the same field.

sections.title: The Change of Basis Matrix (The 'Translator')
sections.content: Explain that moving from Basis B to Basis A requires a matrix P, where the columns are the Basis B vectors expressed in terms of Basis A coordinates. Visualize this as a 'transformation bridge' connecting two different grid overlays on the same 2D plane.
sections.example: To convert coordinates [v]_B to [v]_A, compute [v]_A = P * [v]_B. If Basis B is { (1,1), (0,1) }, the matrix P = [[1, 0], [1, 1]].

sections.title: Visualizing the Inverse
sections.content: Discuss how to go back. If P takes us from B to A, P-inverse takes us from A to B. Show an animation where the coordinate grid 'stretches' and 'shears' to match the new basis.
sections.example: If the robot reports its position in local grid coordinates (Basis B), we multiply by P-inverse to get its position on our global map (Standard Basis A).

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Recap: Change of basis is a change of language, not a change of reality. Emphasize that finding the 'right' basis can simplify complex physics/engineering problems (e.g., diagonalizing matrices).
sections.example: Final shot: A complex vector spinning in space; changing the basis allows us to view the rotation as a simple projection on one axis—making the math 10x easier.

[VideoCritic][section_1] Problem: The axes animation encroaches on the left-side text area, creating visual clutter. Fix: Line 59: self.place_in_area(axes, 'D2', 'F6', scale_factor=0.5) (line=59, object=axes)

[VideoCritic][section_1] Problem: The point 'v' is positioned too close to the origin, causing visual overlap with the axis labels. Fix: Line 62: self.place_at_grid(v, 'E4', scale_factor=0.8) (line=62, object=v)

[VideoCritic][section_1] Problem: The spatial distribution causes the right-side visual elements to look cramped, misaligned with the text. Fix: Line 59: self.place_in_area(axes, 'B3', 'E6', scale_factor=0.6) (line=59, object=axes)

[VideoCritic][section_2] Problem: The basis vectors 'b1' and 'b2' in the first segment obstruct the central visual axis and overlap with the coordinate grid axes. Fix: self.place_at_grid(b1, 'D5', scale_factor=0.6); self.place_at_grid(b2, 'D2', scale_factor=0.6) (line=3, object=b1, b2)

[VideoCritic][section_2] Problem: The grid visual in the second segment lacks clear separation from the lecture text, causing potential readability issues. Fix: self.place_in_area(grid_visual, 'A3', 'F6', scale_factor=0.8) (line=6, object=grid_visual)

[VideoCritic][section_2] Problem: The standard basis labels 'i' and 'j' are too close to the origin, creating a cramped visual style. Fix: self.place_at_grid(i, 'E5', scale_factor=0.9); self.place_at_grid(j, 'B3', scale_factor=0.9) (line=1, object=i, j)

[VideoCritic][section_3] Problem: Matrix P and its label are too close to the left text area, creating visual clutter. Fix: Line 66: self.place_at_grid(p_matrix, 'B4', scale_factor=0.6); Line 74: self.place_at_grid(label, 'B3', scale_factor=0.8) (line=66, object=p_matrix and label)
[VideoCritic][section_3] Problem: Vector v_b is awkwardly positioned relative to the matrix and formula. Fix: Line 82: self.place_at_grid(v_b, 'D4', scale_factor=0.8) (line=82, object=v_b)

[VideoCritic][section_3] Problem: The equation spans too large an area, potentially conflicting with the lecture text flow. Fix: Line 90: self.place_in_area(equation, 'E3', 'F5', scale_factor=0.7) (line=90, object=equation)

[VideoCritic][section_4] Problem: The matrix P and its inverse formula are vertically aligned with the grid visualization, causing the grid animation to overlap and obstruct the P-inverse text as it renders. Fix: Line 64: self.place_at_grid(matrix_p, 'B2', scale_factor=0.9); Line 70: self.place_at_grid(matrix_inv, 'D2', scale_factor=0.9) (line=64, object=matrix_p and matrix_inv)

[VideoCritic][section_4] Problem: The grid animation is currently placed too far to the right, causing it to clip or look detached from the mathematical context while encroaching on the far-right boundary. Fix: Line 76: self.place_in_area(grid_lines, 'B4', 'E6', scale_factor=0.7) (line=76, object=grid_lines)

[VideoCritic][section_4] Problem: The proximity between the text labels and the mathematical objects is currently unbalanced, leading to a cluttered visual flow in the center of the frame. Fix: Line 64: self.place_at_grid(matrix_p, 'B2', scale_factor=1.0); Line 70: self.place_at_grid(matrix_inv, 'D2', scale_factor=1.0) (line=64, object=matrix_p and matrix_inv)

[VideoCritic][section_5] Problem: The vector arrow animation at B5 obstructs visual clarity and encroaches on the central viewing area. Fix: Line 60: self.place_at_grid(group, 'B4', scale_factor=0.9) (line=60, object=group)

[VideoCritic][section_5] Problem: The matrix formula at D5 is placed too far right, creating an unbalanced layout and potential edge clipping. Fix: Line 66: self.place_at_grid(matrix, 'D3', scale_factor=0.8) (line=66, object=matrix)

[VideoCritic][section_5] Problem: Persistent animation elements at the start of the summary block interfere with reading the lecture notes. Fix: Line 5: self.place_in_area(vector, 'E1', 'F2', scale_factor=0.6) (line=5, object=vector)

The axes animation encroaches on the left-side text area. Please adjust: Line 59: self.place_in_area(axes, 'D2', 'F6', scale_factor=0.5). Also, the point 'v' is positioned too close to the origin: Line 62: self.place_at_grid(v, 'E4', scale_factor=0.8). Finally, the spatial distribution makes right-side elements look cramped: Line 59: self.place_in_area(axes, 'B3', 'E6', scale_factor=0.6). Note: Issue 21, 22, 23 covers these, please resolve all.

Basis vectors 'b1' and 'b2' obstruct the central visual axis and grid: self.place_at_grid(b1, 'D5', scale_factor=0.6); self.place_at_grid(b2, 'D2', scale_factor=0.6). Grid visual lacks separation from text: self.place_in_area(grid_visual, 'A3', 'F6', scale_factor=0.8). Standard basis labels 'i' and 'j' too close to origin: self.place_at_grid(i, 'E5', scale_factor=0.9); self.place_at_grid(j, 'B3', scale_factor=0.9). Issues 24, 25, 26 refer.

Matrix P and label too close to left text: Line 66: self.place_at_grid(p_matrix, 'B4', scale_factor=0.6); Line 74: self.place_at_grid(label, 'B3', scale_factor=0.8). Vector v_b is awkwardly positioned: Line 82: self.place_at_grid(v_b, 'D4', scale_factor=0.8). Equation spans too large an area: Line 90: self.place_in_area(equation, 'E3', 'F5', scale_factor=0.7). Issues 27, 28, 29 refer.

Matrix P and inverse formula overlap grid animation: Line 64: self.place_at_grid(matrix_p, 'B2', scale_factor=0.9); Line 70: self.place_at_grid(matrix_inv, 'D2', scale_factor=0.9). Grid animation is too far right/clipped: Line 76: self.place_in_area(grid_lines, 'B4', 'E6', scale_factor=0.7). Fix balance: Line 64: self.place_at_grid(matrix_p, 'B2', scale_factor=1.0); Line 70: self.place_at_grid(matrix_inv, 'D2', scale_factor=1.0). Issues 30, 31, 32 refer.

Vector arrow animation at B5 obstructs view: Line 60: self.place_at_grid(group, 'B4', scale_factor=0.9). Matrix formula at D5 is too far right: Line 66: self.place_at_grid(matrix, 'D3', scale_factor=0.8). Persistent animation at start of summary block interferes with lecture notes: Line 5: self.place_in_area(vector, 'E1', 'F2', scale_factor=0.6). Issues 33, 34, 35 refer.
